name: HR Engagement Platform
description: Built a cross-department engagement strategy and cross-device design system for a 41K-user platform

items.label: Projects reused the Design system across multiple products
Estimated revenue generated across two phases
Faster production time across design and development

legend.app: A mobile app was developed to drive talent engagement and improve company culture.
legend.system: A comprehensive design system was created for the solution.
legend.flow: An experimental user-flow tool was developed to better predict user engagement and analyse rewards balance.

attract.headline: Clients wanted to improve talent retention across every generation
body: They wanted to attract new talents while sustaining the seniors already in the workforce. So our goal was to develop a digital product that speaks to a wide persona range from Gen X to Gen Z.
To better understand the motivations of our targeted users, I collaborated with analysts to map 6 generic personas to pin down their expectations, values, and how they’d interact with the platform.
attract.legend: We gathered generic personas as a base to then analyse their motivations, interests and emotional drives.

cultures.headline: People don't quit jobs. They quit cultures
body: Research showed that toxic environments, feeling unseen, and feeling stuck were three main reasons talents left companies.

Those pain points became our north star for the project. We needed a platform that makes people feel like they're growing, valued, included. We wanted to turn individual actions into collective belonging.

industry.headline: The platform had to adapt to different industries
body: Shipping it as a fixed product meant every client got the same features regardless of what actually fit their culture or industry, so we needed to keep it flexible from the start.
To do so, I decided to establish a flow made of two surveys combined with the project scopes, so the final application would satisfy the initial human needs.
I also built a UI guideline that would let us dial the expression up or down, more playful or more restrained, based on each client's culture.
industry.legend: We built a guide to better define the gamification strategy to better suit each company's culture.

gamification.headline: We build the engagement layer around gamification
body: Many articles defined "Gamification" as the ideal candidate for sustainable engagement. However developing the reward system was only half of the challenge, we also needed a way to sell it and educate clients on the matter.

To do so, I partnered with an analyst who owned the sales and delivery side, while I owned the technical architecture. The numerous exchanges helped keep every technical decision tied to a business lens.
gamification.legend: We split responsibilities according to our expertise, this led to a balanced collaboration where we dove into technical details without losing the initial business goals.

tenure.headline: Should a new hire and a veteran earn the same way?
body: Early on, we considered talent growth and purpose as a central point within our reward system.

As a result we designed the user journey so beginners would focus more on building habits through self-fulfilment, while veterans would be highly rewarded by contribution to the collective engagement.

extend.headline: How do you extend a Design System without bloating it?
body: Since we wanted to reuse this solution across clients, every new component had to be reusable, not client-specific.
However, the real challenge sat on how to educate clients on why some customization could not be done as it would harm the project's scalability.

To answer this, I coupled the design system with a business-oriented guideline, so client would better understand the value of such design system. The guideline was used as a guardrail that we could adapt to each client.

legend.system: I first added necessary components to the library, ensuring they would serve the project and be reused across devices.
legend.strategy: The design system was coupled to a business-oriented guideline, so clients would better understand the design system benefits.

engines.headline: Gamification needed a UX framework, not just a strategy deck
body: Although our understanding of gamification was solid in theory, we lacked a proper framework to apply it to our design and user-journey.
I decided to create three engagement engines that aligned with our initial goals:
list: Social: responsible for team bonding (shared milestones, public recognition).
body2: Each engine became its own set of UI patterns, so a client could dial recognition up, keep rewards subtle, or boost social interaction to better fit their culture.

reframe.headline: Executives didn't want "gamification"
body: The word itself read as gimmicky to stakeholders, they wanted something that felt professional.
We decided to reframe the entire concept as "Reward-Driven Engagement", and built a story around it that would better align with client's initial concerns.

demo.headline: Slides couldn't sell something this complex
body: The concept was too new for sales to pitch on slides alone, so we were asked to build something they could actually show.
I worked with the dev team to code an early prototype so sales could directly showcase basic mechanics. I also got to create a promotional video mixing AI with mockups to bring the pitch to life.

legend.before: Sales reported the initial slides were too abstract and received mitigated feedback from clients.
legend.after: A prototype with basic functions was developed as to directly showcase clients.

restructure.headline: Gamification was competing with the product instead of enhancing it
body: The senior consultant handed me a feature table built from client interests. However the table mixed engagement mechanics with generic app functions which made it hard to leverage engagement in each function.
I collaborated with the analyst to separate gamified mechanics from standard functions, so the gamification mechanics could be plugged into any generic feature instead of fighting it for space.

legend.before: Initially both functions and gamification features were mixed together, which led to an unbalanced reward economy.
legend.after: We decided to segment them into either core functions vs engagement drive to better leverage engagement in each function.

deals.headline: The concept sold twice before it shipped
body: The prototype and demo were convincing enough and helped close two client deals. One of them was confident enough to sign for a phase two that would include additional features and a more comprehensive reward system.

list.headline: Confirming what really matters to clients before deepening research
list.challenge: The reward economy and the R&D journey-mapping tool were more sophisticated than what the client actually used: coins redeemed for gifts.
list.outcome: I now confirm what KPIs matter to the client before scoping investment.

list.headline: Pilot-testing the methodology, not just pitching it
list.challenge: The strategy was grounded in strong research and market trends, but shipped without empirical validation.
list.outcome: Going forward, I would pilot-test surveys and processes like this before rolling them out, to confirm they actually work as intended rather than just sound right.

list.headline: Push for a more cohesive user-journey
list.challenge: Design decisions leaned on leadership preference more than employee-validated needs, and features shipped as disconnected pieces gathered from benchmarks rather than a meaningful journey.
list.outcome: Going forward, I would further exchange with PM and analysts to develop a solid user requirements methodology.
